opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a useful lens, but it has real limits. When we break intelligence into separate abilities, like reading comprehension, math, coding, visual reasoning, or long-term memory, we get something measurable, and that's valuable. You can see where a system is strong and where it's weak instead of collapsing everything into one number that hides the profile. Models are very jagged. They can do graduate-level physics problems and then fail at something a child would find trivial. A decomposition helps you see that jaggedness.

The problem is that intelligence isn't just the sum of its parts. A lot of what makes humans generally capable is how the abilities interact. You need to hold information in memory while you reason over it, switch strategies when one isn't working, notice you're confused, and adapt in an unfamiliar environment. If you test each ability in isolation, with clean, well-specified tasks, you can miss the integration failures, which often show up in long-horizon, open-ended work.

There's also a question of which abilities you choose. Any list reflects a theory of cognition, and if the theory is missing something, like learning on the fly from experience or certain kinds of motor or spatial understanding, the systems can look much closer to "general" than they are. And there's the usual benchmark problem: once something becomes a target, people optimize for it, and the scores drift away from the underlying capability.

So I'd say treat the ability-by-ability view as a diagnostic, not a definition. It tells you where the bottlenecks are, which matters a lot for forecasting and for safety, because a single missing capability can be the thing holding back a big jump in real-world impact. But you also need holistic evaluations: can the system actually do economically meaningful tasks end to end, autonomously, over hours or days? Ideally you look at both, and when they disagree, that's usually where the interesting insight is.

r001.rationale: It says abilities interact and recommends using both ability-by-ability diagnostics and holistic evaluations, communicating that decomposition can coexist with evaluating combinations.

r002.rationale: It discusses economically meaningful end-to-end tasks, but does not mention MMLU, crystallized intelligence, or say that performance on one need not translate to practical competence.

r003.rationale: It says benchmark scores can drift from underlying capability and separately identifies bottlenecks, but does not clearly state that relying solely on benchmarks can obscure those bottlenecks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we don't really have a great way of doing this, and the decomposition approach has some real problems baked into it.

The way the field has mostly operated is: you pick a bunch of tasks, you build a benchmark for each, and you treat the aggregate as a proxy for "intelligence." Math reasoning, coding, reading comprehension, commonsense, and so on. And that's fine as far as it goes, but there are a few issues.

The first is that the abilities aren't actually separable. When you look at the correlation structure across benchmarks, there's usually a dominant general factor, something like the g-factor in human psychometrics. So you end up with these dozens of benchmarks that are all largely measuring the same underlying thing, and you get a false sense of coverage. You think you've mapped out a space when you've really just sampled one dimension many times.

The second is the opposite problem, which is that the things that are actually distinct, or that we care about most, tend to be the ones that are hardest to put in a benchmark. Things like good judgment, knowing when you don't know, being able to do a long-horizon task without drifting off, or having the right values. Those don't decompose neatly into a multiple-choice format, so they get underweighted simply because they're hard to measure. And that creates a distortion where the models get optimized for whatever is legible rather than whatever matters.

The third thing is saturation. Benchmarks have a short half-life now. You put something out, and within a year or two it's at ninety-plus percent, partially because of genuine capability gains and partially because of contamination or targeting. That's part of why we built things like Humanity's Last Exam, to try to get something that's actually at the frontier of human expert knowledge rather than something that's already mostly solved. But even that's a temporary measure. It'll saturate too.

So my view is that you can't really evaluate intelligence as a checklist. What you can do is track capabilities that are tied to concrete consequences. Can it do autonomous cyber operations? Can it meaningfully uplift someone trying to make a biological weapon? Can it do long-horizon ML research on its own? Those are specific, they're decision-relevant, and when the answer flips from no to yes it should actually change what you do. That's a more useful frame than trying to put a single number on general intelligence, which I think is partly a category error anyway.

And I'd add, there's a safety angle here too. If your eval story is "we have a hundred benchmarks and they all look good," that's a lot of false reassurance. The things that go wrong are usually the things you didn't think to measure.

r001.rationale: The response says abilities are not separable and rejects a checklist approach, but does not say that evaluating combinations of abilities is compatible with the decomposition approach.

r002.rationale: It does not mention MMLU or crystallized intelligence, nor state that this may fail to translate into practical-task competence.

r003.rationale: It warns that benchmarks can give a false sense of coverage, underweight hard-to-measure capabilities, and miss the things that go wrong—communicating that benchmark-only views can obscure important capability gaps.

astra-6.text:
I think breaking intelligence into separate abilities is useful, but it can give us a misleading picture if we treat those abilities as independent. You can measure mathematical reasoning, factual knowledge, planning, and so on, but real tasks often require all of those to work together. A system might perform well on each isolated test and still struggle when it has to decide which ability to use, when to use it, and how to recover from a mistake.

There’s also a distinction between possessing a capability and reliably applying it. If a model solves a problem with a very carefully constructed prompt, that tells us something about what it can do. It doesn’t necessarily tell us how well it will perform when the problem is ambiguous or unfamiliar.

So I wouldn’t discard evaluations of individual abilities. They’re useful diagnostics. But I’d complement them with tasks that test how those abilities interact, whether they transfer to new situations, and whether the system can sustain good performance over longer sequences of decisions. A collection of benchmark scores is evidence about intelligence; it isn’t a complete account of it.

r001.rationale: It says individual ability evaluations are useful diagnostics and should be complemented by tasks that test how abilities interact.

r002.rationale: It does not mention MMLU or crystallized intelligence, or state that those measures may fail to predict competence at practical tasks.

r003.rationale: It warns that isolated tests and benchmark scores can give a misleading or incomplete picture, including by concealing difficulty integrating abilities and applying them reliably.

sol-6.1.text:
I think breaking intelligence into separate abilities is useful for measurement, but it can give us a misleading picture if we treat those abilities as independent. You can test mathematical reasoning, factual knowledge, planning, and so on, but what matters in a real situation is often how those capabilities work together. A system might do well on each component and still fail to recognize which capability to use, or fail to carry a solution through over a longer horizon.

There’s also a distinction between being able to solve a problem when it’s clearly presented and being able to identify the problem in the first place. Benchmarks usually supply the question, define the objective, and make it relatively clear what counts as success. The real world often doesn’t do that.

So I’d view a collection of evaluations as evidence about intelligence, rather than a complete definition of it. We still need to ask whether those abilities generalize, whether the system can integrate them in unfamiliar situations, and how reliably it does that. A single aggregate score can obscure a lot of those differences.

r001.rationale: It says separate abilities are useful to measure but must also be assessed for how they work together in real situations.

r002.rationale: It does not mention MMLU, crystallized intelligence, or whether that knowledge translates to practical task competence.

r003.rationale: It warns that evaluations and aggregate scores can obscure differences, and that systems may fail to select or sustain the use of a capability despite doing well on components.
